Design Efficiency, Pseudoquadratic Surfaces, Assurance, and Augmentation

Source: vignettes/v32-design-efficiency-pseudoquadratic-augmentation.Rmd
v32-design-efficiency-pseudoquadratic-augmentation.Rmd

Why compare matrices before planting the experiment?

Experimental cost, time, estimability, and prediction precision can differ substantially among treatment matrices.

The 2002 Agrociencia article by Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza compared numerous agricultural response-surface designs for pseudoquadratic models using integrated response variance, determinant, and trace criteria (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

A central methodological lesson is that design rankings can depend on the criterion.

The determinant criterion in that study did not always agree with trace or integrated prediction-variance criteria.

Version 1.1.0 incorporates that lesson directly: it reports multiple criteria and does not hide their disagreements behind a single best_design() decision.

Learning objectives

After this vignette, the reader should be able to:

  • compute A-, D-, I-, and G-information summaries;
  • compute relative efficiency against a reference matrix;
  • reproduce the run-adjusted comparison convention used in the attached 2002 study;
  • evaluate sensitivity to the prediction region;
  • rank candidates criterion by criterion;
  • combine information with an explicit cost model without pretending cost defines scientific quality;
  • fit identifiable pseudoquadratic fertilizer models;
  • understand the source equation ambiguity documented by the package;
  • add prior information to design evaluation;
  • interpret Bayesian A-, D-, I-, and G-planning criteria;
  • run simulation-based design assurance;
  • augment an existing design sequentially;
  • distinguish information gain from evidence observed after the experiment.

1. A common reference matrix

The article expresses efficiencies relative to a three-level factorial in two or three factors (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

Create the two-factor reference:

f3 <- expand.grid(
  x1 = c(-1, 0, 1),
  x2 = c(-1, 0, 1)
)

For a conventional second-order model this matrix has nine distinct treatment combinations.

2. A CCD candidate 

library(bayesAgriFlow)
ccd <- bayes_ccd(
  c("x1", "x2"),
  center_points = 5
)

3. Classical information summary 

bayes_design_efficiency(ccd)

The output separates:

  • A information;
  • D information;
  • I integrated prediction variance;
  • G maximum prediction variance;
  • trace of the coefficient covariance matrix under unit error variance;
  • determinant of the information matrix;
  • determinant of the corresponding covariance matrix;
  • scaled condition number.

4. Direction of each criterion

The reporting conventions are chosen to reduce ambiguity.

Larger A and D values indicate more coefficient information.

Smaller I and G values indicate lower prediction variance.

The raw trace and covariance determinant are smaller-is-better uncertainty quantities.

Always inspect the definition before comparing numbers from different software.

5. Relative efficiency 

bayes_design_efficiency(
  design = ccd,
  reference = f3,
  style = "standard"
)

The standard D relative value compares normalized D information.

A, I, and G use precision-oriented candidate/reference ratios expressed through the appropriate inverse uncertainty quantity.

6. Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza run adjustment

The source article adjusts relative efficiencies for the number of experimental runs (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

Use:

bayes_design_efficiency(
  ccd,
  reference = f3,
  style = "briones2002"
)

The package explicitly labels this convention.

It should not be mixed silently with normalized D-efficiency definitions from another source.

7. Published benchmark asset

The values printed in Tables 1 and 2 of the attached article are stored as a documentation benchmark.

p <- system.file(
  "extdata",
  "briones_martinez_2002_efficiency.csv",
  package = "bayesAgriFlow"
)
bench <- read.csv(p)
head(bench)

These rows are source-derived benchmark values.

They are not recomputed package outputs.

This distinction is deliberate.

8. What the source reported for two factors

Under average integrated variance across its selected regions and pseudoquadratic models, the source found repeated double square and double square among the most efficient two-factor matrices (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

It also found several A-optimal, San Cristóbal, Thompson central-composite, and related designs above the three-level factorial under that particular criterion.

Those conclusions belong to the model, regions, coding, and efficiency definition used in the article.

They are not universal rankings for every response-surface problem.

9. What the source reported for three factors

For three factors, the A-optimal 31-treatment matrix had the largest average integrated-variance relative efficiency among the designs listed in the article (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

The paper also reported more disagreement among criteria in the three-factor case.

This reinforces the package decision to retain multiple metrics.

10. Design ranking by criterion 

candidates <- list(
  CCD = ccd,
  Factorial3 = f3,
  Aopt = bayes_optimal_design(2, 9, criterion = "A"),
  Dopt = bayes_optimal_design(2, 9, criterion = "D")
)

bayes_design_rank(candidates)

The output has separate ranks for A, D, I, and G.

rank_mean is a descriptive summary only.

It is not a hidden multi-criterion scientific optimum.

11. Why no universal best-design function exists

Parameter estimation and regional prediction are different goals.

A design can perform well for one and less well for another.

The relevant criterion should be declared before observing the responses whenever possible.

12. Prediction region sensitivity

The article evaluated integrated variance over several two-dimensional subregions (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

Version 1.1.0 generalizes that idea.

regions <- list(
  full = list(x1 = c(-1, 1), x2 = c(-1, 1)),
  inner75 = list(x1 = c(-0.75, 0.75), x2 = c(-0.75, 0.75)),
  inner50 = list(x1 = c(-0.50, 0.50), x2 = c(-0.50, 0.50))
)

bayes_design_region_sensitivity(
  ccd,
  regions,
  criterion = "I"
)

13. Why the region matters

A fertilizer recommendation may only be used inside a regulatory, economic, or biologically sensible subset of the mathematical design cube.

Giving all coordinates equal prediction importance can be inappropriate when some settings will never be used.

14. Explicit point clouds as regions

The region can also be supplied as a data frame of points.

set.seed(11)
region_points <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(500, -1, 1),
  x2 = runif(500, -0.6, 0.9)
)

bayes_design_efficiency(
  ccd,
  region = region_points
)

This can approximate an irregular agronomic operating region.

15. Experimental cost

The motivation for compact response-surface designs includes experimental economy.

Version 1.1.0 allows cost to be stated explicitly rather than buried in an informal preference for fewer runs.

bayes_design_cost_efficiency(
  ccd,
  criterion = "I",
  cost_per_run = 100,
  fixed_cost = 500
)

16. Cost is not information

The function reports information per declared cost.

It does not transform a cheap but non-estimable design into a good experiment.

Rank and estimability must be checked first.

17. Compare cost efficiency with a reference 

bayes_design_cost_efficiency(
  ccd,
  criterion = "A",
  cost_per_run = 100,
  fixed_cost = 500,
  reference = f3
)

The cost model can later be expanded to distinguish run types if a project has defensible cost data.

18. Pseudoquadratic models in fertilizer research

The source article emphasizes fractional-degree pseudoquadratic models as potentially useful approximations in fertilizer experiments (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

Version 1.1.0 provides an explicit transformed-quadratic construction.

Define:

zj=xjaj,xj≥0. z_j=x_j^{a_j},\qquad x_j\ge 0.

Then fit a second-order polynomial in the transformed variables z.

19. Why non-negative coding is required

Fractional powers of negative real values are generally not real-valued.

The source study therefore uses factor levels coded on [0,2] for its fractional-exponent calculations (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

The package enforces non-negative inputs for bayes_pseudoquadratic().

20. Teaching pseudoquadratic data 

dp <- bayes_teaching_data("pseudoquadratic")
head(dp)
range(dp$N_code)
range(dp$P_code)

21. Square-root transformed quadratic 

pdes <- bayes_pseudoquadratic(
  data = dp,
  response = "yield",
  factors = c("N_code", "P_code"),
  powers = 0.5
)
pdes

The internal basis contains transformed linear terms, transformed pure quadratic terms, and transformed interactions.

22. Important source-equation note

The printed model equation in the attached 2002 article appears to show the same fractional exponent for a transformed linear term and the corresponding pure term (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

Read literally, that would duplicate model columns and make the parameterization non-identifiable.

Version 1.1.0 does not silently reproduce that duplication.

It uses the identifiable transformed-quadratic interpretation:

zj=xjaj,zj2=xj2aj. z_j=x_j^{a_j},\quad z_j^2=x_j^{2a_j}.

The design object records this interpretation in model_options$source_note.

23. Alternative powers 

pdes_alt <- bayes_pseudoquadratic(
  dp,
  "yield",
  c("N_code", "P_code"),
  powers = c(0.6, 0.8)
)

Different powers define different model bases.

They should be compared as explicit candidate models rather than selected because one yields a preferred agronomic optimum.

24. Fit the pseudoquadratic model 

pfit <- bayes_fit(
  pdes,
  engine = "native",
  draws = 3000,
  seed = 20260826
)
bayes_summary(pfit)

25. Prediction on the original non-negative scale 

pgrid <- expand.grid(
  N_code = seq(0, 2, length.out = 20),
  P_code = seq(0, 2, length.out = 20)
)

ppred <- bayes_predict(pfit, pgrid)
head(ppred$summary)

The hidden transformed columns are rebuilt internally from the original-scale factor values.

26. Canonical geometry for pseudoquadratic models

Canonical analysis is performed in transformed z coordinates.

bayes_rsm_canonical(pfit)

This is explicitly labeled because a stationary coordinate in transformed space is not the same quantity as the original x coordinate.

For practical recommendations, bounded optimization on the original non-negative factor scale is often easier to communicate.

27. Bounded pseudoquadratic optimum 

bayes_rsm_optimum(
  pfit,
  bounds = list(
    N_code = c(0, 2),
    P_code = c(0, 2)
  ),
  max_draws = 300
)

The optimization evaluates the transformed basis from original x coordinates, so the reported factor values remain on the supplied scale.

28. Classical design information ignores prior knowledge

Traditional information criteria derive from the design matrix and assumed error structure.

Bayesian planning can additionally encode genuine prior information.

For a Gaussian linear basis with prior covariance V0, a simple planning covariance is:

Vpost=(V0−1+XTX/σ2)−1. V_{post}=\left(V_0^{-1}+X^TX/\sigma^2\right)^{-1}.

29. Prior-informed information 

bayes_design_information(
  ccd,
  prior_sd = 2.5,
  sigma = 1
)

The result reports posterior-covariance analogues of A, D, I, and G criteria.

30. Prior sensitivity in planning 

rbind(
  weak = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 5, sigma = 1),
  moderate = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 2, sigma = 1),
  strong = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 0.8, sigma = 1)
)

A design should not be advertised as Bayesian-optimal without stating the prior and noise assumptions used to define that optimality.

31. Noise sensitivity 

rbind(
  sigma05 = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 2.5, sigma = 0.5),
  sigma10 = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 2.5, sigma = 1.0),
  sigma20 = bayes_design_information(ccd, prior_sd = 2.5, sigma = 2.0)
)

32. Bayesian assurance

Assurance is a pre-posterior probability of meeting a declared future-analysis target under specified design, prior, and noise assumptions.

It is not the posterior probability observed after the experiment.

33. Precision assurance 

bayes_rsm_assurance(
  ccd,
  n_sim = 500,
  target = "precision",
  precision_threshold = 0.5,
  seed = 20260826
)

The precision target asks whether the planned posterior coefficient SDs remain below the specified threshold.

34. Curvature assurance 

bayes_rsm_assurance(
  ccd,
  n_sim = 300,
  target = "curvature",
  curvature_threshold = 0.10,
  curvature_probability = 0.95,
  posterior_draws = 300,
  seed = 20260826
)

For each simulated future experiment, posterior coefficient draws are transformed into canonical eigenvalues.

Success requires the posterior probability of practically relevant curvature to exceed the declared probability target.

This is not a Bayes factor.

35. Interior-optimum assurance 

bayes_rsm_assurance(
  ccd,
  region = list(x1 = c(-1.5, 1.5), x2 = c(-1.5, 1.5)),
  n_sim = 300,
  target = "interior_optimum",
  interior_probability = 0.80,
  posterior_draws = 300,
  seed = 20260826
)

This asks whether a future posterior is likely to assign enough probability to a stationary point inside the declared region.

36. Assurance depends on assumptions

Always report:

  • coefficient prior;
  • residual SD assumption;
  • target definition;
  • practical curvature threshold;
  • probability threshold;
  • prediction region;
  • number of simulations;
  • random seed.

An assurance number without these assumptions is incomplete.

37. Sequential augmentation

Suppose an experiment already exists but more runs can be added.

aug <- bayes_rsm_augment(
  ccd,
  n_add = 2,
  criterion = "I",
  candidate_levels = c(-1.5, -1, 0, 1, 1.5),
  seed = 20260826
)
aug

The function does not alter observed responses.

It proposes additional candidate points based on the stated information objective.

38. D-based augmentation 

bayes_rsm_augment(
  ccd,
  n_add = 2,
  criterion = "D"
)

This targets joint coefficient information.

39. Bayesian-I augmentation 

bayes_rsm_augment(
  ccd,
  n_add = 2,
  criterion = "BayesI",
  prior_sd = 2,
  sigma = 1
)

This targets prior-informed integrated posterior prediction variance.

40. Augmentation is a decision

The statistically best next point may be impossible to implement.

Candidate sets should encode feasible agronomic treatments before optimization.

Do not generate impossible fertilizer rates and then ask the field team to make them feasible after the fact.

41. Link to value of information

Information criteria quantify statistical precision.

Value-of-information analysis quantifies improvement in a downstream decision utility.

These are not interchangeable.

A future extension can use the existing bayes_value_of_information() layer to choose additional experiments based directly on expected decision gain rather than only covariance reduction.

42. Legacy agricultural matrices

The package includes inst/metadata/advanced_design_status_1.1.0.csv.

It records which design families have native generators and which are retained only as reference/import targets.

Double Square, Double Cube, San Cristóbal, and Plan Puebla remain reference-only until their coordinate definitions are checked against appropriate primary design sources.

The article benchmark is still useful for teaching historical efficiency comparisons (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

43. Reproducibility versus historical reconstruction

A historical result should not be described as reproduced merely because a modern matrix has a similar name.

True reproduction requires the same:

  • coordinates;
  • coding;
  • model basis;
  • exponent grid;
  • integration region;
  • run-count adjustment;
  • criterion definition.

Version 1.1.0 stores enough provenance to make these distinctions explicit.

44. Design-efficiency reporting template

For a manuscript or technical report, state:

  1. design family and number of runs;
  2. factor coding;
  3. model basis;
  4. region of integration;
  5. A/D/I/G definitions;
  6. reference design for relative efficiency;
  7. run-count adjustment, if any;
  8. cost model, if used;
  9. prior and residual SD assumptions for Bayesian criteria;
  10. assurance target and simulation settings;
  11. augmentation objective and candidate set.

45. A complete pre-experimental workflow 

ccd <- bayes_ccd(c("N", "P"), center_points = 5)

audit <- bayes_rsm_audit(ccd)

comparison <- bayes_compare_designs(
  list(
    CCD = ccd,
    Aopt = bayes_optimal_design(2, 9, "A"),
    Dopt = bayes_optimal_design(2, 9, "D")
  ),
  reference = expand.grid(N = c(-1,0,1), P = c(-1,0,1))
)

information <- bayes_design_information(
  ccd,
  prior_sd = 2,
  sigma = 1
)

assurance <- bayes_rsm_assurance(
  ccd,
  target = "interior_optimum",
  n_sim = 500,
  posterior_draws = 300
)

46. A complete post-data workflow 

d <- bayes_teaching_data("ccd")
fit <- bayes_fit(
  bayes_rsm(d, "yield", c("coded_N", "coded_P")),
  draws = 4000
)

bayes_summary(fit)
bayes_pp_check(fit)
bayes_rsm_canonical(fit)
bayes_rsm_optimum(
  fit,
  list(coded_N = c(-1.5,1.5), coded_P = c(-1.5,1.5))
)

47. Scientific boundaries

Version 1.1.0 does not claim that every historical agricultural matrix is implemented.

It does not claim that pseudoquadratic models are always superior to ordinary quadratics.

It does not claim that D-optimality is equivalent to prediction optimality.

It does not claim that prior-informed information criteria are prior-free.

It does not turn assurance into observed evidence.

These boundaries are part of the implementation, not footnotes added later.

Summary

The design-efficiency layer completes the pre-experimental side of the bayesAgriFlow response-surface workflow.

Classical matrix geometry, regional prediction precision, experimental cost, prior information, and simulation-based assurance can now be examined before responses are collected.

After data collection, the same package carries uncertainty through posterior response surfaces, canonical geometry, optimization, and decision analysis.

That continuity is the main purpose of the 1.1.0 Advanced Experimental Designs module.

Briones-Encinia, Florencio, and Ángel Martínez-Garza. 2002. “Eficiencia de Algunos Diseños Experimentales En La Estimación de Una Superficie de Respuesta.” Agrociencia 36 (2): 201–10.
